title: The Garland That Bound and Released
subtitle: Satyabhama's Punyaka rite and the gift to Narada
story:
The garland Satyabhama lifted over Krishna's head was not meant as decoration. Flowers and all, it was a binding — the knot of a rite that would hand her husband to a wandering sage and then buy him back again, all within the same afternoon.

It began with a summons. Krishna thought of Narada, and the sage appeared as though the thought itself were a road. Satyabhama invited him to accept the Punyaka ceremonies, and when the appointed hour came, she and Krishna bathed the great muni, anointed him with scents, hung garlands on him, and fed him with their own hands. Then the rite proper began. The lucky damsel set a garland of flowers around Krishna's neck and bound him to the Parijata, the heavenly tree that grew in Dwaraka. With his permission she dedicated him to Narada, and then she gave away her gifts: sesame seeds that gleamed like jewels, gold mixed with rice and other plants, mountains of gold, and a thousand cows — wealth poured out in such measure that the ceremony looked less like worship than like a festival of giving. The women of the household looked on as the sage accepted it all, and the joke that was already forming hung in the air.

Narada accepted everything, delighted. "O Keshava," he said, "given by Satya together with water, you have become mine. Follow me, and do what I say."

"This is the first stage," Krishna answered, and began to follow him.

The sage walked a few paces, cut various jokes, and said, "Wait here, I am going." Then, instead of going, he lifted the garland from Krishna's neck. "To release yourself," he said, "give me a Kapila cow with her calf, and the skin of a black antelope filled with sesame seeds and gold. This means of release has been laid down by the god whose emblem is the bull."

"So be it," said Krishna, and offered the fee on the spot. Then he smiled at the muni. "Narada, you who are conversant with religion, I have been greatly pleased with you. Ask for a boon, and I will grant it."

Narada asked that the eternal Vishnu might always remain pleased with him, and grant him habitation with him; and that if he were ever born again, he might be born of no woman, and as a Brahmana. "So it will be," said Krishna, and the sage was content — for the lord's promise to the wandering singer of heaven had been spoken, and everyone who heard it knew that it would hold.

The rite did not end with the release. Satyabhama had invited all sixteen thousand of Krishna's wives to the Punyaka ceremony, and when it closed she distributed among them the celestial garments and ornaments that Shachi, Indra's queen, had once given to Vasudeva — finery from the very court of heaven, handed out in Dwaraka as a bride's gift to a household. And the Parijata, at Krishna's command, began to display its own accomplishments, flowering and working its wonders while friends and relations gathered to witness the power of the tree.

It became a festival. Krishna brought the Pandavas, with Pritha, Draupadi and Subhadra; Shrutasrava came with her son, and Bhishmaka with his; and other friends and relations arrived as well. For a year Krishna stayed in Dwaraka, happy in the company of Arjuna and the ladies of his household, the days turning gently around the blooming tree, which flowered in Dwaraka as though it had never left heaven.

At the end of that year he carried the Parijata back to the city of the celestials — returning the tree to heaven, and with it, in some measure, the peace between the two brothers who had lately faced each other in battle.
reflection: The whole rite runs on a divine joke: the lord of the universe is bound by a garland, sold for gold and cows, and ransomed back at a price fixed by Shiva. Krishna plays along without once breaking the mood, and the ceremony ends in generosity instead of solemnity — devotion, in this telling, is not afraid to laugh at itself.
next_story_tease: When the tree came home to heaven, Krishna would make a vow before Indra that set a ten-day countdown to war.
